source.title: Factorization Results for Left Polynomials in Some Associative Real Algebras: State of the Art, Applications, and Open Questions

accepted.question_text: Let R be a finite-dimensional associative real involutive algebra with involution γ, and let C be a left polynomial over R with norm polynomial ν(C)=Cγ(C)=γ(C)C. When ν(C)=0, which such polynomials admit a linear-factor factorization C=c_n(t−h_1)(t−h_2)⋯(t−h_n), and what criteria characterize their factorizability?

evidence.quote: We say that the polynomialC ∈R[t] of degreen ≥ 1 admits a factorizationif there exist ring elementscn, h1, h2, ..., hn such thatC =cn(t −h1)(t −h2) · · ·(t −hn).
ForC ∈R[t], condition (1) implies that thenorm polynomialν(C) := Cγ (C) = γ(C)C of C is in R[t].
Ifν(C) = 0, no suitable fractional linear parametrization exists. Polynomials with the propertyν(C) = 0 are not covered in this text. Their factorizability requires a separate investigation.

accepted.question_text: Let R be a finite-dimensional associative real involutive algebra and let R^γ[t] consist of left polynomials C satisfying γ(C)C=Cγ(C)∈ℝ[t]. Algorithm 2 factors a monic polynomial by choosing a quadratic real factor M of ν(C), computing a zero h=czero(C,M) of the left remainder lrem(C,M), dividing by t−h, and recursing. Beyond division rings, what necessary and sufficient conditions ensure that this algorithm succeeds, and how can one decide whether C admits a linear-factor factorization when the algorithm fails for some choices of the quadratic factors?

evidence.quote: Theorem 3 below covers the case of division rings (real numbers, complex numbers and quaternions by Frobenius’ Theorem) but in its formulation and proof we do not make direct use of properties of these number systems. The reason is that the corresponding Algorithm 2 may make sense in the presence of non-invertible elements as well. Variants and generalizations of Theorem 3 and Algorithm 2 with weaker assumptions are given in Section 6.

accepted.question_text: Let C=P+εQ be a dual-quaternion motion polynomial in DH[t], with P,Q∈H[t], ν(C)∈ℝ[t], and ν(C)≠0. Generic motion polynomials have mrpf P=1; non-generic ones have mrpf P≠1. For non-generic motion polynomials, what general criteria determine whether C itself admits a factorization into linear factors, rather than only whether a suitable multiple CS with S∈ℝ[t] or CD with D∈H[t] admits a factorization?

evidence.quote: A polynomial C = P +εQ ∈ DH[t] with P, Q ∈ H[t] is called amotion polynomial if ν(C) ∈ R[t] and ν(C) ̸= 0. It is calledgeneric if mrpfP = 1.
A generic motion polynomial C = P +εQ ∈ DH[t] with P, Q ∈ H[t] admits a factorization.

If mrpfP ̸= 1, general criteria on existence of factorizations are diﬃcult to formulate. However, we would like to mention recent results by [8, 10] that ensure existence of factorizations for suitable multiples of not necessarily generic but bounded motion polynomials.
There exists a polynomialS ∈ R[t] of degree degS ≤ deg mrpfP such thatCS admits a factor- ization.
If gcd(P,ν (Q)) = 1 there exists a polynomialD ∈ H[t] of degreedegD = 1 2 deg mrpfP such that CD admits a factorization.

accepted.question_text: Let C=P+εQ be an unbounded motion polynomial in DH[t], meaning that mrpf P has at least one real zero. Which unbounded motion polynomials can be made factorable by multiplication with a real polynomial S∈ℝ[t] or a quaternion polynomial D∈H[t], or by a rational reparameterization t=A/B that replaces C by B^deg(C)C(A/B)?

evidence.quote: A motion polynomialC = P +εQ with P, Q ∈ H[t] is called bounded if mrpfP has no real zeros andunbounded otherwise.
If C is an unbounded motion polynomial, existence of a factorization is not guaranteed, not even after multiplication with a real polynomialS ∈ R[t] or a quaternion polynomialD ∈ H[t].

accepted.question_text: Let C be a monic non-motion polynomial in DH[t], or more generally a monic polynomial in Cl(p,q,1)[t], whose primal part A factors as A=(t−a_1)(t−a_2)⋯(t−a_n). After writing C=(t−a_1−b_1)(t−a_2−b_2)⋯(t−a_n−b_n) with unknown dual-part coefficients b_i and comparing coefficients, one obtains a square linear system. What sufficient criteria guarantee solvability of this linear system, and therefore existence of a factorization of C? More broadly, how should the algebra, geometry, and kinematic interpretation of cases with unique, infinitely many, or no solutions be characterized?
accepted.context_brief: Projection factorization criteria for non-motion polynomials

evidence.quote: Assume now that the primal part of the monic polynomialC admits a factorization inCℓ(p,q,0), that is, A = (t −a1)(t −a2) · · ·(t −an) with a1, a2, ..., an ∈Cℓ(p,q,0). We make the ansatz (11) C = (t −a1 −b1)(t −a2 −b2) · · ·(t −an −bn) with yet undetermined coeﬃcientsb1,b2, ..., bn of vanishing primal part.

Comparing coeﬃcients on both sides of (11) yields a system of linear equations for the unknown real coeﬃcients ofb1, b2, ..., bn. The number of equations and the number of unknowns both equal(m + 1)n.

If the primal part of a monic polynomialC ∈ Cℓ(p,q,1) admits a factorization, a factorization ofC exists if the system of(m + 1)n linear equations in the same number of unknowns arising from comparing coeﬃcients of (11) has solutions.

Generically, the solution to the linear system is unique but we already encountered cases with inﬁnitely many solutions or with no solution at all (Examples 7 and 8). The algebra and geometry of factorization of non-motion polynomials in DH[t] (and in particular a kinematic interpretation) occurs in the theses [9, 11] but numerous open issues remain.
In particular, suﬃcient criteria for existence of factorizations, that is, solvability of the system of linear equations arising from (11), would be desirable.
